Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them. According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan , 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives. "Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW. She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections. stories.article_text_excerpt: Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities By James Landale Reporting from Zaporizhzhia oblast Published 15 September 2026 Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way. His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb. But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta. And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present. "If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can." Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. "Millions of people are facing hunger," said Radovan, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "And one thing is clear: The climate crisis is threatening the entire world. No country can tackle it alone." Radovan opened the debate on the federal government's proposed 2027 budget for her ministry with a stark assessment. The budget is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year, falling from just over €10 billion to just under €9.5 billion ($10.9 billion). In 2022, it stood at nearly €14 billion, meaning that the ministry's budget has been reduced by roughly one-third over the past half decade.
